extracted.subtask_description: Information and post-accident regulatory/operational requirements, design changes, and training expectations related to the Boeing 737 MAX (especially MCAS) and the aircraft's return-to-service and airworthiness certification. Covers FAA airworthiness directives, required tests, training, and design-disclosure issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: MCAS system purpose and operation
rubrics_metrics.description: MCAS on the 737 MAX was designed to mimic the pitching behavior of the previous generation ... by pushing down the aircraft nose from an elevated angle of attack (AoA) by automatically adjusting the horizontal stabilizer and trim tab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains intended function (protect against high AoA / potential stall) and notes operational details (automatically adjusts stabilizer/trim). Context includes that Boeing asserted MCAS was not an anti-stall system and that pilot movement of the control column did not disable MCAS in the MAX's original implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of MCAS in flight manuals and design differences
rubrics_metrics.description: During certification of the MAX, Boeing requested and received permission from the FAA to remove a description of MCAS from the aircraft manual, leaving pilots unaware of the system when the airplane entered service in 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied requirement/best-practice: critical flight-control features and design differences (e.g., MCAS) should be included in Flight Crew Operating Manual (FCOM), Quick Reference Handbook (QRH), and Design Differences Tables so pilots and operators are informed. The page documents this omission as a failure of disclosure and a focus of subsequent criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: AoA-sensor redundancy for MCAS activation
rubrics_metrics.description: FAA Airworthiness Directive (2020) approved design changes requiring input from two AoA sensors for MCAS activation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory requirement introduced after the accidents to reduce single-sensor failure risk. Presented as a mandatory design change for each MAX aircraft as part of return-to-service conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate MCAS repeated activation
rubrics_metrics.description: FAA Airworthiness Directive required elimination of the system's ability to repeatedly activate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design change mandated to prevent MCAS from repeatedly re-engaging after corrective pilot action; part of the FAA-approved set of fixes for continued airworthiness and safe operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot override capability for MCAS
rubrics_metrics.description: FAA-mandated changes include allowing pilots to override the system if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses original MAX behavior where pilot control column movement did not disable MCAS. Guidance implies automated protections must be defeatable/overridable by pilots through normal procedures or trim/cutout mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: AoA sensor system test and validation flight before airworthiness certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: For each aircraft, the FAA would issue the airworthiness certificate, without delegation to Boeing, upon completion of an AoA sensor system test and a validation test flight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural/certification requirement: specific functional testing and a validation flight must be completed and inspected by the FAA prior to issuance of an airworthiness certificate; denotes direct FAA oversight rather than delegated conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAA-issued simulator training requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA also required new simulator training specific to the MAX, including recovering from a simulated MCAS failure, before pilots may operate the MAX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training standard introduced as part of return-to-service: simulators and scenario-based training addressing MCAS failure modes are mandatory. The page contrasts this with prior policy where simulator training was not required because FAA accepted Boeing's claim of similarity to the NG.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency AD: inclusion of service bulletin and immediate review
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA issued an emergency airworthiness directive, 2018-23-51, requiring the bulletin's inclusion in the flight manuals, and that pilots immediately review the new information provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational/procedural requirement following the Lion Air crash: affected operators had to incorporate Boeing's supplementary bulletin into manuals and ensure flight crews reviewed the procedures (e.g., non-normal runaway trim) immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer architecture redundancy requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing overhauled the computer architecture of the flight controls to provide greater redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical standard: improved redundancy in flight-control electronics and architectures was mandated/implemented to mitigate single-point failures contributing to unsafe behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: AoA warning system functionality and truthful disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing had knowingly withheld knowledge, for at least a year before the Lion Air crash, that a system to warn of a possible AoA malfunction did not work as advertised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation/requirement: safety-critical warning systems (e.g., AoA disagreement/warning) must function as claimed and manufacturers/operators must disclose limitations or failures to regulators and operators; failure to do so undermines safety and regulatory trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of pilot non-normal procedures (runaway trim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The supplementary service bulletin says warnings triggered by erroneous AoA data could cause the pitch trim system to repeatedly push down the nose of the airplane and referred pilots to a 'non-normal runaway trim' procedure as resolution, specifying a narrow window of a few seconds before the system would reactivate and pitch the nose down again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational-crew-procedure requirement: non-normal procedures must be practicable and effective given system behavior (e.g., narrow reactivation windows may make procedures difficult). The page highlights that pilots followed recommended procedure in Ethiopian crash but the design/behavior still produced fatal outcomes, prompting redesign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory disclosure of design changes to certification authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents criticism that Boeing and the FAA omitted information about MCAS from communications with the public, 737 MAX customers, and MAX pilots, and notes 'Exclusive: Boeing kept FAA in the dark on key 737 MAX design changes - U.S. IG report'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory standard/best practice: manufacturers must disclose substantive design changes to certification authorities and supporting documentation; failure to disclose led to oversight failures, investigations, and formal reports (House final committee, IG report).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory acceptance of model similarity affects training requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the accidents, simulator training on the MAX was not required, because the FAA accepted Boeing's position that the MAX was sufficiently similar to the previous 737 series, the NG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: regulators' judgment that a new variant is 'sufficiently similar' can waive additional training requirements; the MAX case demonstrates that such determinations must be carefully validated because they directly impact crew preparedness for system differences.
